hooks: My six-year-old just called me out on my composition.
Spent thirty minutes today explaining negative space to a kid playing with Legos.
Kids don't know what 'rule of thirds' means, but they feel it.
"Why can't the green Lego guy just stand in the middle?"
I block scenes for a living, but today a six-year-old schooled me.
We worry so much about framing theory, but children just get it.
Teaching composition to my son using green Legos and a plastic castle.
Why do we lose our natural sense of visual balance as we grow up?
My son's Lego castle has better framing than my first short film.
No camera, no monitor, just two Lego blocks and a lesson in framing.

caption_variations: My son asked why the green Lego guy couldn’t just stand in the exact middle of his castle. We ended up having a half-hour chat about "room to breathe" and why corners feel alive. He didn't care about the jargon, but he got the geometry instantly.

I spend weeks blocking scenes for actors, but my kid just solved a framing issue with two Legos. He wanted his green toy in the center. I showed him how the corner gives it "room to breathe." Now his Lego castle looks like an A24 frame.

"Why can't he just stand in the middle?" my son asked, holding a green Lego figure. Instead of a quick answer, we spent thirty minutes on the living room floor talking about visual breathing room. Kids are natural directors before we ruin them with theory.

We overcomplicate composition. My six-year-old wanted his Lego knight dead center in the castle. We shifted it to the side, talked about the empty space, and his eyes lit up. He got the geometry without needing the words.

It takes years of film school to learn what a child understands intuitively. Today, a conversation about a green Lego guy's placement in a plastic castle reminded me why we need to let our frames breathe.

No monitors, no red ink, just a Sunday morning on the floor with my son. He asked why his green Lego guy shouldn't go dead center. Thirty minutes later, he was talking about negative space without even knowing the word for it.

If you want to test your understanding of visual design, try explaining it to a kid with Legos. My son wanted his hero right in the middle. We moved him to the corner, and the whole story of his plastic castle changed.

Kids don't need text books to understand tension. My son moved his green Lego man to the edge of the castle wall because "it felt like he was looking for someone." Honestly, his framing instinct is sharper than mine.

A green Lego guy, a plastic castle, and a lesson in keeping things simple. My son didn't care about the term "negative space," but he immediately saw how moving the toy to the side made the castle feel huge.
Sometimes the best directing notes happen on the living room rug. My son wanted his Lego toy in the center. I told him to leave some room to breathe. He got the visual math instantly.
comment_bait_questions: At what point in your life did you start noticing how things were framed, rather than just what was in the frame?
Do you remember the first film or scene that made you realize the middle of the frame isn't always the most powerful spot?
How do you unlearn all the technical rules when you're actually on set and just need to trust your gut?
What's the simplest way you've ever had to explain a complex visual concept to someone who doesn't work in film?
Do you find yourself naturally centering your subjects when you shoot, or do you instinctively look for the corners?

Zero risk of sounding like generic marketing because it is a direct quote from a child, immediately establishing authenticity.
